standard_prerequisites.name: Infinite Ramsey theorem, in the article's own big-Ramsey-degree form
standard_prerequisites.statement: For every n and every finite colouring of the n-element subsets of the naturals there is an infinite subset on which the colouring is constant; the article restates this as T(n, omega) = 1 at source lines 241-251.
standard_prerequisites.use: Applied twice in the counted proof, to the four-tuple colouring of the pairs of omega (source line 507) and, in the sibling arguments of the same section, to colourings of the naturals.

standard_prerequisites.name: Order equivalence and copies of the integers
standard_prerequisites.statement: Two ordered sets are order-equivalent when an order-preserving bijection exists between them; the ordered set zeta is the integers with their natural order, and a subset of zeta is order-equivalent to zeta exactly when it has neither a least nor a greatest element and is unbounded in both directions.
standard_prerequisites.use: Both directions of the counted proof rebuild or test a subset H of zeta that is order-equivalent to zeta, and the lower bound uses that such an H must contain positive elements, negative elements and pairs of both signs.
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: definitions at source lines 172-196 and 213-216, retained as context

standard_prerequisites.name: Elementary manipulations of Z with signs, absolute values and parity
standard_prerequisites.statement: Every integer is either a nonnegative integer or the negative of one; the absolute value of a negative integer is its negation; an infinite subset of the naturals can be split by the parity of its indices.
standard_prerequisites.use: Building the four sign combinations of a pair, comparing absolute values in the four cases of the lower-bound colouring and alternating the signs of the sequence h_0, h_1, ... when the copy of zeta is rebuilt.

core_obligations: Encode an arbitrary colouring of the two-element subsets of the integers by the four-tuple colouring of the two-element subsets of the naturals that records the four sign combinations, and apply the article's Ramsey statement on the naturals to obtain one infinite set on which that four-tuple colouring is constant.

Rebuild a copy of the integers from that homogeneous set by taking the negatives of the even-indexed elements and the odd-indexed elements themselves, and verify that every pair of the rebuilt set is one of the four encoded pairs and that the parity alternation keeps the two absolute values distinct, which the four-tuple bookkeeping alone does not control.

For the lower bound, define the four-colouring of the pairs of the integers by the signs of the two entries together with the comparison of their absolute values, and prove that every subset of the integers that is order-equivalent to the integers contains a pair in each of the four cases, so that no order-equivalent copy can be three-homogeneous.

proof_roadmap.step: Upper bound: replace the colouring of the pairs of zeta by the four-tuple colouring COL'(x,y) = (COL(-x,-y), COL(-x,y), COL(x,-y), COL(x,y)) on pairs x < y of omega, apply Ramsey to get an infinite 1-homogeneous G, and rebuild H = {-h_i : i even} + {h_i : i odd}, which is order-equivalent to zeta and uses at most the four recorded colours.
Lower bound: colour a pair by the four cases given by the signs of its two entries and, when the signs differ, by the comparison of the two absolute values.
For an arbitrary H that is order-equivalent to zeta, exhibit a pair of H in each of the four cases, so all four colours occur on every order-equivalent copy and no such copy is three-homogeneous.

difficulty_reason: The counted statement fixes the big Ramsey degree of the ordered set of integers for pairs, T(2,zeta) = 4, so both a four-colour upper bound for an arbitrary finite colouring and a four-colouring that no order-equivalent copy can reduce have to be produced, and the two directions use different constructions. The upper bound at source lines 499-513 replaces the colouring of the pairs of zeta by the four-tuple colouring of the pairs of omega that records the four sign combinations, and then rebuilds a copy of zeta from the homogeneous set G by alternating signs with the parity of the index, H = {-h_i : i even} + {h_i : i odd}; the author's aside at source line 511 states that exactly this alternation is what guarantees that the two absolute values are distinct, a condition the four-tuple bookkeeping does not control by itself. The lower bound at source lines 515-537 needs a case analysis that a routine appeal to Ramsey's theorem does not supply: the four-colouring is defined by the signs of the two entries and by the comparison of their absolute values, and for an arbitrary H that is order-equivalent to zeta one must first see that H contains a pair in each of the four cases before all four colours can be claimed. Applying Ramsey's theorem directly to zeta is not available here, because the theorem is stated for the naturals and the reconstruction of a zeta-copy is the actual work.

compared.difference: The only public item of this article counts the omega-squared example T(2, omega^2) = 4, whose upper and lower bounds use the coefficient and colouring-rule machinery for ordinals below omega^omega. This target is about the ordered set of integers, which is not an ordinal and is not order-equivalent to omega^2, and its proof is the article's separate direct argument with a sign-alternating reconstruction; neither statement implies the other and no step is shared.

That card counts the exact big Ramsey degree of finite powers omega^d through canonical coefficient patterns and the finite pattern count. This target counts a degree for the integers, where no coefficient pattern exists, so the counting objects and the proofs are disjoint.

That card counts the general equality for every ordinal alpha below omega^omega, with the mixed-exponent block construction and the generalized colouring rules. The integers are not an ordinal at all, so T(2,zeta) lies outside its scope; the article itself announces the integers result in a separate section and proves it without the ordinal machinery.

compared.label: uncounted siblings inside the same article
compared.difference: The general integers theorem of the same article, T(n,zeta) = 2^n at source lines 553-591, is deliberately NOT counted: its printed lower bound ends by leaving the absence of a zeta-(2^n - 1)-homogeneous set to the reader at source lines 588-589, so the article's printed proof is incomplete there. The n = 1 sibling T(1,zeta) = 2 at source lines 473-493 has its own complete proof but is the same integers counting object with one element and is subsumed by the general theorem, so it is not counted either; the counted n = 2 theorem is the one case that carries a complete printed proof of both bounds.
